cards.title: Audio CD bait pieces: cheap, long-form, and low-production
cards.summary: Audio CDs make low-cost information bait pieces that prospects can consume while driving, exercising or doing chores.
cards.use_when: Choosing an information premium format (lead magnet) for a lead-generation campaign and weighing audio against print or video.
steps: Pick audio when the prospect base commutes or does chores and can listen passively; audio doesn't demand the dedicated attention a DVD does.

Do not force brevity for its own sake: if the content is pure, useful information, a 30- to 90-minute recording has worked for promoting seminars and consulting/copywriting services. Short 10-20 minute pieces are also viable.
Repurpose existing material: record a live presentation, speech, work meeting or industry event, then edit it in a studio.

Budget from the source's examples: $200-$400 plus travel to hire someone with professional-quality equipment to record a presentation; $75-$95/hour for studio time, typically under half a day; about $1.25 per unit to duplicate with a laser-printed label in a vinyl case or sleeve. Verify current prices with vendors.
Make the content genuinely useful on its own so it works as information bait rather than a thinly veiled pitch.
caveats: The cost figures are older examples from the source's experience, not current quotes; get real vendor pricing.
Audio's advantage is passive listenability, so it suits topics that work without visuals.
Long runtime only works if the information is useful; a 90-minute ad will not hold attention.

cards.title: DVD/video bait pieces: low production values are now accepted online
cards.summary: Marketing video can be shot cheaply because web viewers accept amateur production values, unlike the old broadcast-TV quality standard.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to produce a video premium or lead-generation asset and estimating production budget.
steps: Recognize the shift: conventional wisdom once held that marketing video had to match broadcast-TV production values or viewers would reject it as inferior.

The source's claim is that this has changed: most small internet marketers post homemade clips with minimal production values, and audiences watch millions of amateur videos on YouTube and similar sites, so web users now accept low production values.
Shoot your own video with a handheld digital camera or webcam to avoid spending hundreds or thousands on professional production.

If you do hire out: expect at least $1,000-$2,000 for a professional to record you on location or in a studio; a full production with sets and special effects can run $5,000-$15,000 or more for an eight-minute video. Duplicating 1,000 copies of an 8-minute video runs about $2.50 each with a cardboard box and typed label; plastic boxes and four-color packaging cost more.
If you want production training, the source points to AWAI's video-marketing program; verify current offerings before citing it.
caveats: The budget figures are the source's examples and may be outdated; confirm current quotes.
This source is a copyright-protected book; the AWAI promotion inside it is marketing copy, not independent evidence.
Low production values may not suit every audience or premium; the source's point is about web video acceptance specifically.

cards.title: Software and CD/USB data premiums: high perceived value at near-zero cost
cards.summary: Software demos, data files, and interactive CDs carry perceived value of $49-$499 while costing about a dollar to deliver.
cards.use_when: Selling a business or software-related product to PC-using prospects and choosing a premium or bait piece.
steps: Offer demos or evaluation copies of software on CD or as a download—a standard lead-generation tactic among software marketers.
Exploit the perceived-value gap: a program can sell for $49 to $499 or more, while your cost per premium is about a dollar with a CD, or near zero as an online download.

Make the disc navigable: Computron Software's marketing director Alex Plavocos organized the information on his marketing CD using Excel so prospects could find the specific product, service, or application they cared about.
Use CD-ROMs or USB drives for sales and informational presentations prospects view on a PC.

Consider data files, spreadsheets, calculators, or utility software as the premium when your audience is technical; a disk of utilities doubled response in one Novell NetWare promotion cited by the source.
Skip this format for audiences without computers or who are not computer literate.
caveats: Only appropriate for PC-using audiences; the source explicitly says not to use it with non-computer-literate prospects.
Software premium value depends on relevance to the prospect's work, not just the list price.
Compatibility and licensing of bundled software are practical issues to verify.

cards.title: Get free or cheap content for bait pieces from reprints
cards.summary: Reprint rights, association publications, and uncopyrighted U.S. government booklets supply bait-piece content at little or no creation cost.
cards.use_when: Needing a booklet, tip sheet or special report as an information premium but lacking budget or staff to write and design one.
steps: Write a feature story on your topic for an industry trade journal, then reprint the article as a tip sheet or booklet, eliminating the need to write, typeset and design an original piece.
Secure reprint rights: type 'First rights only' in the upper left corner of the first page of your manuscript so that after the magazine runs it you own all rights.
Label the reprint a 'tip sheet' or 'special report' rather than an 'article reprint'—the former convey higher perceived value—and cite the original publication and date in small type.
Reprint existing material relevant to your product or market: professional societies and trade associations often let members reprint informative publications free or for a reasonable sum.

Add your own front and back cover with logo, company name, description and contact information when reprinting. One orthodontist reprinted a health booklet with his office address and phone number, added a personal cover letter, and mailed it to potential patients with good results.

Use uncopyrighted U.S. government publications: they may be reprinted for promotional purposes, with acknowledgment requested but not required. A radon-testing firm offers a government report on 'Radon in the Home' with the firm's name and phone number imprinted.
If you are an agent, representative, distributor or dealer, ask your manufacturer or wholesaler for literature you can reprint or add your label to.
caveats: Always confirm reprint rights or obtain permission; 'First rights only' governs first-publication rights, not all uses.
Generic reprints fit products with broad appeal; for a highly specialized technical product you probably must create your own report.
The source often recommends custom-created premiums anyway because original publications can be more interesting and better tied to the product.

cards.title: Answer five common objections to free booklet offers
cards.summary: Objections that free-booklet offers are clichéd, overused or competitor-matched are refuted by response results, not by originality.
cards.use_when: A stakeholder resists adding a free booklet/report offer to a campaign because it seems unoriginal or crowded out.
steps: On 'it's a cliché': the source's position is that originality is unimportant; what matters is that free booklet offers generate more leads per ad or mailing and lower marketing cost, and this works consistently across industries.

On 'it's overused': the source argues the opposite effect often occurs—prospects in an industry get used to seeing free booklet offers and seek out such ads; an ad without a bait piece is more likely to be skipped.

On 'competitors already offer one': bait pieces are almost never a branding strategy or USP, so a competitor's booklet is irrelevant and even evidence the tactic works. Either choose a different topic that still promotes your product, or produce a better booklet on the same topic—add tips competitors omit, glossaries, charts, conversion tables, bibliographies, checklists, resource names and addresses, graphs, illustrations, and inside detail competitors keep secret. Pick a clearly different title; similar titles confuse prospects.

On 'prospects have too much to read': a prospect drowning in paperwork will still request a report that speaks to a pressing problem, e.g. '6 Proven Ways to Cut Energy Costs in Your Plant This Year.' Even if the prospect requests but never reads it, the offer still generated an inquiry that would otherwise not exist, and the selling process can begin.

On 'we'll get freebie seekers': qualify up front (see the lead-qualification card) rather than dropping the offer. Without a free booklet offer, prospects may respond only to competitors' ads that do offer booklets.
caveats: These are the source's assertions from direct-response experience, not independently verified benchmark data.
The source notes freebies are a real risk; the answer is qualification, not abandoning the tactic.
Booklet content must remain relevant and tailored to prospect needs or it will not overcome reading inertia.

cards.title: Qualify leads to reduce freebie seekers
cards.summary: Use friction, screening questions and delayed gifts to filter low-intent inquiries while keeping the info premium free.
cards.use_when: A free information premium is generating many unqualified or freebie-seeker leads that waste fulfillment time.
steps: Ask prospects to answer questions about themselves or their business on the reply card (e.g. 'What type of business are you in?' or 'What is your immediate need?').
Make them fill out a survey or questionnaire.
Require postage on the return envelope or postcard (self-addressed, stamped envelope).
Tell prospects you will not fulfill inquiries that omit a phone number.
Use the phrase 'Serious inquiries only, please.'

Charge a nominal fee for catalogs, brochures or literature, or ask $1-$2 to cover handling—but see the caveats and the pricing card, since the source generally advises against charging for the bait piece itself.
Do not stress guarantees, money-back offers, free offers, and risk-free trials or estimates.
If you offer a premium gift, do not send it in response to the inquiry: give it in person at the sales meeting or send it only when the prospect purchases.
caveats: Charging for the bait piece badly hurt one mentor's ad: inquiries fell from dozens to two or three per ad and produced no business.
The source recommends free bait pieces for 99.99% of marketers; qualification friction is the preferred lever, with charging as a rare exception.
Added friction lowers total response volume—accept the tradeoff deliberately.

cards.title: Price the bait piece: free beats fee almost always
cards.summary: For lead generation the bait piece should be free; charging screens out qualified prospects as well as freebie seekers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to charge for a booklet, report or information kit used to generate leads.
steps: Default to free for booklets and reports used to generate leads; charging dramatically decreases response and slows lead flow.
Recognize the exception: if your primary business is selling books or reports by mail and the premium is meant to build a mailing list, charging can make sense.
Reject the theory that paying $5 makes a prospect better qualified to buy your widget—it mainly adds the trouble of writing a check, which blocks qualified prospects who would otherwise respond.
Qualify by asking questions (business type, immediate need) on the coupon or reply card instead of by price.

Choose from the source's basic bait-piece options: free to prospects who call or mail the reply card; free only to qualified prospects; free with a self-addressed, stamped envelope; free with SASE plus $1-$2 handling; a flat price such as $5; free to qualified prospects and $5 to everyone else; or a free CD/DVD with $5.95 charged to a credit card for shipping and handling. Free download fulfillment reduces costs to practically zero.

The source's mentor SR ran small Wall Street Journal display ads for a free copywriting information kit: dozens of inquiries per ad with some turning into business. When he required just three dollars, response fell to two or three per ad and produced no business.
caveats: Recovering printing and distribution cost via SASE plus $1-$2 is possible but not recommended by the source.
Charging can be right if you are actually in the business of selling that information product.
Online downloads change the cost math but not the response logic.

cards.title: Soft vs. hard offers in lead generation
cards.summary: Soft offers generate leads with free information; hard offers capture hot prospects ready to buy and result in a meeting.
cards.use_when: Designing a lead-generation campaign and choosing whether to ask for an information request or a sales conversation.
steps: Define the soft offer: it offers information—a product brochure, white paper, or other free content—to qualified prospects who could benefit but are not ready to buy, getting them to raise their hand.

Define the hard offer: it captures inquiries from hot prospects with an immediate need who want to buy now rather than later, and results in a face-to-face or telephone meeting between seller and buyer.

Use the source's submarine metaphor: prospects are submerged most of the time and surface occasionally; the soft offer ferrets out submerged prospects, while the hard offer spots hot prospects swimming on the surface.
Match the offer type to readiness: a prospect actively solving a specific problem or handling a particular application is a hard-offer candidate.
Expect hard offers to be evaluated by meetings booked and converted to sales, not by raw lead volume.
caveats: The source's framing is for lead generation/sales pipelines, including B2B and service businesses; ecommerce marketers should translate a booked meeting into whatever committed next step fits a purchase path.
Hard offers require follow-up capacity; a booked meeting you cannot service is not a win.

cards.title: Hard offer rule 1: never say 'salesperson'
cards.summary: Repackage the 'have a salesperson call' offer with a prospect-oriented title to lift response.
cards.use_when: Writing the reply option for a hard offer that asks a lead to accept a call or visit.
steps: Note the problem: the check-off 'Have a salesperson call me' is the most widely used hard offer, but few prospects select it because 'salesperson' signals high-pressure selling that benefits the seller, not the buyer.

Replace 'salesperson' with a prospect-oriented title such as Account Representative, Senior Consultant, Technical Specialist, Account Manager, Account Supervisor, Industry Specialist, Program Manager, Program Planner, [product] Specialist, or [application] Specialist—or create your own appropriate title.

Match the title to the subject matter: financial services should say 'Have a financial consultant call' or 'Have a financial planner call' (only if your salespeople truly are planners); a relational database should say 'Have a database specialist call'; a consultant teaching social-networking selling should say 'Have a social networking specialist call.'
Keep the title honest: it should describe what the person actually does.
Rewrite other copy so the contact reads as a helpful meeting rather than a sell job.
caveats: The source does not recommend renaming the role without changing how the contact actually goes; a warm title over a hard-sell call will not hold up.
Savvy buyers may still recognize the offer type; the gain is in framing for the majority.

cards.title: Hard offer rule 2: don't offer a 'sales presentation'
cards.summary: Frame the first appointment as a free consultation, analysis, audit or briefing because the meeting itself has value to the buyer.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for the initial appointment a hard offer asks the prospect to accept.
steps: Avoid the words sales call, sales pitch and sales presentation, which carry the negative connotation of 'sales.'

Offer instead one of: initial appointment, free no-obligation consultation, free estimate, free analysis, needs assessment, audit, exploratory meeting, evaluation of their requirements, initial planning session, free demonstration, free executive briefing, or free seminar.

Write the offer as, for example: 'Please have a technical consultant call to arrange a free analysis of my network requirements. I understand there is no cost for this initial analysis—and no obligation.'

Ground the reframe in the real value of the first meeting: price quotes give a benchmark against other bids, printers may share production pointers, and a financial planner must answer questions to demonstrate expertise—value the buyer keeps even without hiring you.
Use this framing to highlight the value of the contact itself instead of asking for a sales opportunity.
caveats: The reframe must be truthful; if the meeting is solely a pitch, the softer words will damage trust.
Free analysis or briefing language promises real substance, so the salesperson must deliver it.

cards.title: Hard offer rule 3: don't charge for the first meeting
cards.summary: Free initial consultations win against competitors who charge, especially when your copy removes suspicion of hidden fees.
cards.use_when: Structuring a hard offer in a field where some vendors charge for estimates, drawings or initial consultations.
steps: Assume you need the business: if you had more leads than you could handle, you would not be prospecting, so offer the initial meeting or conversation free.
For marginal-value prospects, make the free meeting a phone call; reserve travel for potentially lucrative accounts.
State plainly that the meeting or consultation is free—this alone can beat competitors who charge.

Learn from the landscape-architect example: three firms quoted equivalent prices; two included a free preliminary drawing, the third charged $100 for his drawing, so his quote showed no drawing and he lost the job despite seeming reasonable.
Because generous offers breed suspicion of hidden charges, stress in copy: 'This initial consultation is absolutely free, with no obligation of any kind.'
caveats: The source's advice is for active prospecting where you need new business; a firm already at capacity has different economics.
Some fields legitimately charge for preliminary design work; the source's point is that a free first meeting is an advantage when you need pipeline.

cards.title: Hard offer rule 4: attach a quantifiable value to the free meeting
cards.summary: Make the free consultation feel exclusive and valuable by naming a specific, quantified deliverable.
cards.use_when: Designing a hard offer that needs to overcome prospect inertia and stand out from generic free consultations.
steps: Offer the initial meeting free, but present it as an exclusive, valuable service rather than generic free stuff, which people do not get excited about.
Package the value as a named deliverable with a stated worth—e.g. a free analysis 'worth $100 or $1,000.'

Model on the Timeplex 'free network topology analysis': the rep visited with laptop and proprietary network design software, sketched the prospect's network layout, clicked 'optimize' to reconfigure the network with Timeplex multiplexers, and the software calculated monthly line-cost savings and ROI of adding the network elements.
Copy promised 'a FREE network topology analysis that can reduce your monthly line costs 10% to 20% or more.' The source reports this was hard to resist and extremely successful for Timeplex.
Make the deliverable the prospect keeps even if they do not buy.
caveats: The Timeplex results are a case example, not a promised benchmark; effect depends on the relevance of the analysis tool to the buyer's problem.
Any dollar value or savings percentage you state must be defensible for your product, or it damages credibility.

cards.title: Hard offer rule 5: state no obligation, repeatedly
cards.summary: Spell out that accepting a free offer creates no obligation, in both the letter and the reply form.
cards.use_when: Writing copy for any free consultation, estimate or information offer where prospects may suspect strings.
steps: Repeat the no-obligation message in the sales letter and again on the reply form.
Address the 'too good to be true' reflex directly: prospects need assurance that meeting with you or replying does not obligate them to buy or pay.

Use plain phrases such as: No obligation; No commitment; No risk; Risk-free; No strings attached; There's no obligation of any kind; There's nothing to buy; You pay nothing; You won't be billed; Without charge.
Do not assume prospects already understand this—state it plainly.
caveats: Overuse can read as protesting too much; keep the assurances concrete and tied to the offer.
The promise must be honored in follow-up; high-pressure follow-up invalidates the stated no-obligation terms.

cards.title: Make the offer a designed element, not boilerplate
cards.summary: Confusing, unfair or illogical offer terms quietly cost refunds, trust and response, so work out the terms deliberately.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the offer and guarantee language in a direct-response promotion.
steps: Do not lift closing and offer copy from previous promotions without checking whether the offer and its wording still make sense.

Watch for the prorated 'unmailed issues' refund problem: if a publisher offers both bill-me and pay-with-order, a prorated refund on unmailed issues gives bill-me customers a free issue while cash-with-order customers pay for the issue they received—an incentive against paying up front, the opposite of the publisher's goal.
Fix it by offering a full money-back guarantee within the first 30 days and a prorated refund thereafter, so the first issue is effectively free either way.
Aim for language that cannot possibly be misunderstood; the source warns nothing damages business reputation worse than a customer who misunderstood the offer and feels cheated when refused a refund.

Audit gray areas like 'lifetime guarantee' (whose lifetime? negligence? boredom?), 'full refund on the unused portion' (the source notes some consumers read 'full' as all their money back), and 'free issue' (it is free only if you do not become a subscriber—'risk-free issue' or 'no-risk issue' is more accurate).
If you truly refund everything, say so unambiguously, e.g. 'We'll refund your entire subscription fee in full' or 'We'll refund every penny you paid.'
caveats: The publisher refund behavior described is the source's observation of a 'surprising number' of publishers, not all.

A truly free first issue requires giving 13 issues for the price of 12; the source notes few publishers do this, though an evergreen first issue in a welcome kit makes it easy for a how-to newsletter.

cards.title: Premium structure for bill-me versus payment-with-order offers
cards.summary: Withhold premiums until payment, use modified bill-me terms, and avoid choice-stacking to protect pay-up rates.
cards.use_when: Structuring premiums with a bill-me option, or deciding whether to include bill-me in a B2B or mail-order offer.
steps: Guard against the classic bill-me risk: the subscriber takes the free gift, cancels, pays nothing and keeps the great freebie.

Phrase the bill-me option as: 'Bill me. (Bonus gift sent upon receipt of payment.)' The subscriber could still pay, get the bonus, cancel within 30 days, get a refund, and keep the premium—but that is a lot of trouble for a free special report, so more low-intent respondents drop out.

Use the modified bill-me: 'Bill me. (NOTE: Product not shipped until payment is received.)' This lets the buyer respond without payment and route an invoice through company accounting while protecting you from shipping unpaid product.
Variant: ship the product right away but state 'Bonus Gift is shipped when payment in full for your order is received by us.'
You may also require return of the premium with the product for a refund—useful when the premium is costly to you.

Reduce non-buyers further by asking prospects to initial or sign the order card or provide a purchase order number. For phone and online orders you cannot get a signature but can still ask for a PO number. Do not require an actual purchase order: the number is sufficient, and demanding paperwork loses sales from busy buyers.
Avoid offering a choice among premiums. The source observes alternate-premium choice schemes seldom work because more choices mean more deliberation, and a decision deferred is a decision not made.
Do not offer a bestselling book as a premium—many recipients already own it.
caveats: Bill-me offers commonly lift front-end response but the true measure is how many buyers pay; the source notes gross revenue after no-pays can be less than cash-with-order.

The source's opinion is that B2B direct marketing usually should include a soft bill-me option because companies are not set up to issue advance checks and may defect to more flexible competitors—not a universal rule for consumer sales.
In consumer mail order, hard offer only is viable, especially at low price points where chasing a $12 past-due balance does not pay.
The source's part-time consumer mail-order business with payment-with-order has worked without a bill-me option; test for your own case.

cards.title: B2B offer structure: pair hard payment with a conditional bill-me
cards.summary: Business buyers expect to receive then pay, so offer both a pay-up-front and a bill-me path, with shipment protection.
cards.use_when: Selling to businesses by direct mail or catalog where the buyer's company has its own purchasing process.
steps: Recognize the buyer's situation: B2B recipients order for their company, not personally, and most are not set up to issue advance checks—their normal flow is purchase order, receive product, get invoice, then pay, often in 60 or 90 days.
If your selling method forces business buyers against their company system, they may find buying too difficult or not worth the aggravation and go to a more flexible competitor.
Include a soft bill-me option alongside the hard payment-with-order option.

Use the classic soft offer wording as a starting point: 'We'll send you our product and bill you. If you like it, keep it and pay the bill. If you don't, return it, tear up the invoice, and owe nothing.'
If the product is expensive or easily damaged, substitute the modified bill-me: invoice first and do not ship until payment is received.
Keep the reply mechanics light: do not force prospects to read instructions or fine print or complete complicated paperwork—more required work lowers response.
caveats: The source says demanding payment up front from business buyers may make prospects unable to get an advance check issued at all.
Even modified bill-me options add administrative steps; weigh the paperwork against your margins.
The B2B/lead-generation setting is the source's scope; ecommerce equivalents (purchase orders, net terms for business accounts) should be tested rather than assumed.

cards.title: Choose a premium format with real perceived value
cards.summary: Premiums work when they are wanted, formatted for the audience, and cheap for you to fulfill.
cards.use_when: Selecting a premium for a newsletter, subscription or info-product promotion.
steps: Super-premium: a special report that delivers all or most of the information, secrets or strategies promised in the mailing—e.g. a magalog offering 'Grow Up to 1,000% Richer in the Great Stock Market Panic of 2002' on nearly every other page of a 24-page magalog.
Owner's manual: explains how to use the service for maximum results (e.g. options trading terms such as puts vs. calls and trade types such as straddles).
Vertical premium: an in-depth report on one specific area rather than the big picture (e.g. a supply chain management or ERP report for an IT newsletter).
Resource guide: a mini-directory of vendors, suppliers, associations and websites with addresses, phones, e-mail and URLs.
Surveys: subscriber survey results are highly interesting to potential subscribers—a salary survey premium lifted response to Hospital Admitting Monthly's control mailing by 50%.
'Best of's': collect a dozen popular columns, e.g. regulatory or legal case columns.

Other formats: e-zines, e-alerts, searchable online back-issue archives, forums and chat groups, weekly telephone hotlines, early conference invitations with a subscriber discount, transcripts of seminars/webinars/speeches, audio CDs and DVDs (videos carry higher perceived value, but the source prefers audiotapes because busy people listen in the car), CD-ROMs for multimedia, software (high perceived value, e.g. a trading program or a simple cost-calculator spreadsheet), and three-ring binders for shelf-value newsletters.

Merchandise is common for consumer magazines (Business Week's solar calculator, Sports Illustrated's swimsuit-shoot video) but seldom used in newsletter promotions; Release 1.0's baseball cap was a payment-with-order premium.
Check the editor's magnum opus caveat: a bestselling book is a poor premium because many recipients already own it, and a cheap newsletter is better served by a higher-perceived-value item.
caveats: Choice among multiple premiums tends to hurt response; pick one strong premium.
The 50% survey-premium lift is a single case example, not a benchmark.
Perceived value must exceed fulfillment cost to make the premium economical.

cards.title: Six characteristics of an irresistible offer
cards.summary: Response rises with how different, desirable, high-perceived-value, brand-dramatizing, easy and low-risk your offer is.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or rewriting an offer before launching a direct-response campaign.
steps: Make it different or unique: Bill Jayme's package launching New York magazine proposed a sweepstakes where the prize was dinner at Gracie Mansion with the mayor—sweepstakes existed, but not that prize. The Sovereign Society offered a free Swiss bank account where other investment newsletters offered free special reports; Advertising Age's control premium was a ceramic mug imprinted with a mock Ad Age cover personalized to read 'Jan Smith Chosen as Marketing Genius of the Year.'

Make it desirable: the Sports Illustrated swimsuit video, or a disk of Novell NetWare utilities whose promotion doubled response rates—the outer envelope read 'Yours FREE!—5 Powerful Programs to Help You Manage Your Novell NetWare Network More Efficiently and Easily.' Contrast a financial newsletter renewal premium of playing cards with the editor's picture on them—it flopped, because who would want that.

Maximize perceived value relative to fulfillment cost: software sells for $49-$300+ but costs about a dollar on CD. Playing cards have a perceived value of about a dollar against a $79 newsletter renewal, so they did not motivate. IBM's Olympic pin probably cost a buck, but copy hinted it could become a collectible, creating the impression of higher value.

Dramatize the brand or USP: the free Swiss bank account reinforced offshore investing's core symbol. Where the link is not obvious, find one in copy—Newsweek's free AM/FM radio premium was framed against the magazine's in-depth coverage: radio gives the fastest headlines, Newsweek gives the news in depth.
Make it easy to take advantage of, minimizing prospect effort.
Whether you use a premium or a content offer, when something is free say plainly that it is free.
caveats: These are illustrative cases, not guarantees of matching results.
The source's own caveat: uniqueness alone fails if nobody wants the item—desirability comes first.
Contrived connections between premium and product can read as gimmicky; the Newsweek example worked because the copy made a real distinction between media.

Some marketers using audio CDs think that briefer is better and limit the message to 10 or 20 minutes. But if the audio contains pure, useful information, it can be much longer. I have been successful promoting both my seminars and my consulting and copywriting services using audio CDs that are 30 to 90 minutes long. Prospects must set aside valuable time to watch a DVD. But they can listen to your audio CD while driving the car, exercising, or doing household chores. Audio CDs do not require the high level of production that videos do. You can record a live presentation or speech given at work, a meeting, or an industry event, edit it in a studio, and offer it as an attractive bait piece. What will all this cost? To hire someone with professional-quality equipment to record a presentation costs $200 to $400 plus travel expenses. Studio time goes for $75 to $95 per hour, and should take less than half a day. To duplicate my audio CDs with a laser-printed label in a vinyl case or sleeve costs about $1.25 per unit. Create Visual Excitement With a DVD Videos are another story.

 You can expect to pay a professional at least $1,000 or $2,000 to record you on location or in a studio. If you want a fullblown production with sets and special effects, an eight-minute video can cost $5,000 to $15,000 or more, just for production. The cost to duplicate 1,000 copies of an eight-minute video is about $2.50 per cassette with a cardboard box and typed label. Plastic boxes and four-color packaging can run much higher. But do you need to hire expensive pros to create your marketing videos? Or can you do it yourself with a camcorder or even a webcam? For many years, conventional wisdom was that the quality of a marketing video had to be equal or nearly equal to the quality of broadcast television. Reason: The viewer is accustomed to watching TV, and therefore rejects anything with lesser production values as inferior and cheesy. But all that has changed. The overwhelming majority of small Internet marketers who post videos on their sites shoot homemade clips, with minimal production values, using hand-held digital cameras. Internet users watch millions of videos on YouTube and other video-sharing sites, all similarly produced by amateurs. As a result, the Internet user is very accepting of low production values on Web videos. So you can shoot your own video and eliminate the need to spend hundreds or thousands of dollars to hire a professional. _____________________________ If you’d like to find out more about how to use video to market your products and services online, check out American Writers & Artists Inc.’s (AWAI) program Marketing With Video Online for Profit at www.awaionline.com/video-marketing/. AWAI teamed up with award-winning videographer, Jessica Kizorek, to give you everything you need to: Write, shoot, edit, and distribute a video and make it look professional, even if you have no experience or have only used YouTube™ for fun in the past; Why people expect more from the marketing materials and advertisements they see, and what you can do to deliver on their expectations; What it takes to persuade someone to take a desired action in a video and how that translates into a video script and shooting; How to measure the success of your video (even a simple YouTube™ video); The legal considerations to keep in mind when shooting and distributing your videos; Business models they can use to build a successful video marketing business; Video-marketing techniques for marketing your services, including a “vlog” (video blog); and How you can make sure you have a never-ending stream of clients ready to pay for your services and much more! _____________________________ An Offer With Incredibly High Perceived Value Sales and informational presentations can be put on CDs or USB drives that the prospect can view using a personal computer. Disks and flash drives containing software or data files have a high perceived value and, therefore, make effective bait pieces. They work well with businesspeople, PC users, and others who have access to a personal computer. I would not use them for audiences that don’t have computers or are not computer literate. Many software marketers generating leads offer demos or evaluation copies of their software on CD or via download as the bait piece. Alex Plavocos, Marketing Director of Computron Software, used Excel to organize the information on his marketing CD. This enabled prospects to easily find information on the particular product, service, or application they were interested in. Software has an extraordinarily high ratio of perceived value to actual cost. Since a software program can sell for $49 to $499 or more, the consumer considers it a valuable product. Yet your cost per premium is about a dollar with a CD, or virtually zero if you offer a download online. In fact, this is one of the few direct-response rules that works almost every time. In virtually every campaign where I have added a free booklet offer to the marketing program, sales lead generation has increased substantially and marketing costs were reduced. I know of few other strategies that are so basic, simple, and easy to use while consistently delivering such excellent results. Despite this, many marketers avoid using free booklet offers, based largely on the following erroneous beliefs. If you are not using the bait piece strategy because of one of these fears, this list may be helpful in overcoming your particular objection. The five erroneous beliefs are: 1. “It’s a cliché.” The number one reason marketers avoid free booklet offers is that they think it’s old hat and are looking for something original. They say to me: “Offering a free booklet isn’t original. Can’t you think of something more creative?” My answer is simple: So what if it’s old hat? So what if it’s a formula? What’s important is that they will generate more leads per ad or mailing, producing more inquiries and more sales while lowering marketing costs. 2. “It’s overused.” Another common objection is, “I like the idea, but free booklet offers are so overused in our industry. While there are some marketing techniques that do lose effectiveness in the face of clutter and overuse, the free booklet offer is not one of them. But the bait piece itself is almost never a branding strategy or unique selling proposition (USP). The right strategy is to go ahead with your own booklet and either (1) choose a topic that’s different but still helps promote your product or (2) choose the same topic and produce a report or booklet that’s better. How do you make your booklet better? Give tips and strategies the competition does not. Include a helpful glossary, charts, conversion tables, bibliography, checklists, names and addresses of resources, graphs, and other useful references. Use pictures and illustrations to make your point clear. Reveal inside information and details the competition keeps secret. Even if the topic is similar, select a title that’s clearly different from the competition’s. Tell prospects you will not fulfill inquiries if they do not provide their phone number. The soft offer is designed to generate leads from qualified prospects — folks who could surely benefit from your product but are not ready to buy it. It does this by offering them information: a product brochure, white paper, or other free content. The hard offer captures inquiries from hot prospects who have an immediate need and want to buy now instead of later. It results in a face-toface or telephone meeting between the seller and the potential buyer. A marketing manager once told me that prospects are like submarines: They are submerged most of the time and surface only occasionally. The soft offer ferrets out prospects who are submerged by getting them to raise their hands and say, “I might be interested. Tell me more.” But the hot prospect has surfaced. She is actively looking for a product or service to solve a specific problem, fill a pressing need, or handle a particular application. The hard offer is the weapon that helps us spot hot prospects “swimming on the surface” and reel them in. In this chapter, we’ll review five time-tested rules for creating winning hard offers that capture more hot prospects that you can meet with and convert into sales. Rule 1: Do Not Involve “Salespeople.” A typical hard offer in lead generation is a check-off box on the business reply card or ad coupon that says, “Have a salesperson call me.” By choosing this offer option, the prospect is saying, “I have sufficient interest in your product or service that I am willing to have your salesperson make a presentation to me or at least chat with me over the phone for a few minutes.” This is a more aggressive, active response toward initiating the next step in the selling process than the soft offer of “Send me a brochure.” “Have a salesperson call” is probably the most widely used hard offer in lead generation. It paves the way for the in-person sales visit that, for many marketers, is a crucial step in getting the prospect to buy their product or service. In many cases, however, very few prospects select this offer option. Reason: Prospects don’t view salespeople as helpful or beneficial. In fact, the word salesperson signals to the prospect that sales pressure will be exerted — something most prospects want to avoid. The word “salesperson” has a negative connotation, implying that the prospect will be subjected to high-pressure selling tactics aimed at benefiting the seller, not the buyer. The solution is to repackage the “Have a salesperson call me” offer, using skillful copywriting and a change in tactics, to convert what is perceived as a sell job into what is perceived as a meeting that will be beneficial and helpful for the prospect. In a nutshell, this is done by replacing the words sell and sales with words that are more prospectoriented. To start with, do not use the term salesperson when referring to the person who will contact or follow up with the prospect. Replace salesperson with any of the following (or create your own title, as appropriate): Account Representative Senior Consultant Technical Specialist Account Manager Account Supervisor Industry Specialist Program Manager Program Planner [name of product] Specialist [description of application] Specialist For example, if you are selling financial services, don’t say, “Have a sales representative call.” Instead, say: “Have a financial consultant call” or “Have a financial planner call” (if your salespeople are truly financial planners). If you are selling a relational database, say, “Have a database specialist call.” If you are a consultant teaching firms how to sell by using social networking, say “Have a social networking specialist call.” Rule 2: Do Not Offer to Do a “Sales Presentation.” Do not use the words sales call, sales pitch, or sales presentation when referring to the initial appointment you are seeking with the prospect, because of the negative connotation of the word sales. Instead of a sales call or sales presentation, suggest to prospects that they contact you to arrange one of the following: Initial appointment Free, no-obligation consultation Free estimate Free analysis Needs assessment Audit Exploratory meeting Evaluation of their requirements Initial planning session Free demonstration Free executive briefing Free seminar Your hard offer might now read: Please have a technical consultant call to arrange a free analysis of my network requirements. I understand there is no cost for this initial analysis — and no obligation. If you phrase your offer this way (or in a similar fashion), you will get more response than if you simply say, “Have a salesperson call” or “Call me to arrange a sales presentation.” Why does this technique work so well? If you think about it, you’ll realize that any initial contact between buyer and seller is not merely a selling opportunity for the marketer — it has value to the buyer independent of whether he buys the product or service. For example, if a printer makes a presentation and gives you a price quotation, that price information is of value even if you do not hire the printer, since it provides a benchmark against which you can judge other quotes. You might also gain some helpful pointers on the print production process, and the printer is not compensated for giving this knowledge to you unless you actually hire him to do the job. Say you have an initial meeting with a financial planner during which you ask questions about investment options, your financial situation, and so on. In order to convince you that she is knowledgeable, the financial planner will probably answer many of those questions. You can put that information to work even if you decide not to hire that particular person. Therefore, the initial sales meeting has value inherent in the meeting itself and independent of the product or service. The strategy of offering a “free consultation by our expert,” as opposed to the traditional “sales presentation by our salesperson,” simply recognizes this inherent value — and it increases response by highlighting the value of the initial meeting or contact itself, rather than asking for a sales opportunity. If you always had more leads than you could ever hope to handle, you would not need to proactively generate more. Given that you want or need new business, you can get more appointments by offering the initial meeting or conversation for free. Some prospects may represent an account so potentially lucrative that it is worth traveling to meet them. With prospects whose value is more marginal, you may decide that the only way you can “meet” with them for free is over the phone. When your prospect requests an initial meeting, make it clear that the meeting or consultation is free. This alone may give you an advantage over your competitors, some of whom may charge for the first meeting. For instance, we once called three landscape architects to get a quote on landscaping the front lawn of a home we owned. All three have good reputations in our county. It entitles you to 12 monthly issues, which works out to $8 per issue. After three issues, you cancel. If the publisher offers both a bill-me option (soft offer) as well as a payment with order option (hard offer), such a prorated refund guarantee actually gives his customers an incentive not to take the hard offer and pay up front — the opposite of what the publisher desires. If you demand payment up front, the prospect may not even know how to get the accounting department to issue and send you an advance check. Therefore, when selling to businesses, you should offer both a soft bill-me option as well as a hard payment-with-order option. Fortunately, there is a way to structure an offer that meets your business customer’s needs as well as your own requirements. It is done by extending a traditional hard offer (payment up front), as well as a second one that is conditional, rather than a pure “soft” bill-me offer. The traditional soft offer says, “We’ll send you our product and bill you. If you like it, you can keep it and pay the bill. If you don’t, you may return it, tear up the invoice, and you will not owe us any money.” Perhaps your product is expensive or easily damaged, and you are afraid that people will take advantage of you by ordering the product, keeping it, and not paying for it. One solution is to use a modified bill-me offer, in which you agree to send an invoice but do not ship the product until the invoice is processed and payment is received. This would read as follows: [ ] Bill me. (NOTE: Product not shipped until payment is received.) The modified bill-me is similar to a soft offer in that it allows the prospect to respond without enclosing any payment and to receive an invoice from you that he can put through the system for payment. At the same time, it is similar to a hard offer in that the product is not shipped until it is paid for. A variation of the modified bill-me is to agree to ship the product right away but to withhold shipment of any gift item or other premium until payment is received. There is a danger, if your premium is too attractive, that people will send for your product on a bill-me basis just to get the premium, then return the product and keep the free gift. To prevent this, you use a modified bill-me offer as follows: [ ] Bill me. (NOTE: Bonus Gift is shipped when payment in full for your order is received by us.) Even if you allow prospects to keep the premium if they return the product, this modified bill-me offer cuts down on freebie seekers. It requires ordering and paying for the product in order to get the gift, and few will go to that trouble just to get a free item from you — unless the premium is truly fantastic. You can go even further and state in your offer that, if they don’t want to keep the product and decide to return it for a refund, they must return the premium as well as the product. This provides an added degree of protection and is useful when the premium is fairly costly to you. Another way to modify the bill-me offer so that you reduce the number of prospects who send for the product and don’t buy it is to ask prospects to initial or sign the order card or provide a purchase order number or actual purchase order. For example: [ ] Bill me. Our purchase order number is: ______________ Signature (required for all bill-me orders): ______________ For phone and online orders, you can’t get a signature, but you can still ask for a purchase order number. I recommend that you avoid requiring prospects to send you an actual purchase order. The purchase order number itself is sufficient. If you insist on getting an actual purchase order, you will lose sales from prospects who are too busy to generate the paperwork. In general, your mailings should never force prospects to read a lot of instructions or fine print or fill out a lot of complicated paperwork. The more work you force your prospect to do to respond to your mailing, the lower your response will be. The two basic categories of premiums are merchandise and free content or “information premiums” (as discussed in Chapter 2). The legendary adman David Ogilvy, after working as a chef in the kitchen of a French hotel, began his career in marketing by selling stoves door to door. He offered the homemaker six cooking lessons for three guineas, but gave the lessons free if you bought the stove. (Source: Kenneth Roman, The King of Madison Avenue: David Ogilvy and the Making of Modern Advertising, page 40) Offering one or more premiums is a standard ploy used in direct mail and online marketing to sell magazines, newsletter subscriptions, and other information products. But which premiums work best? What are your choices? Most premiums for newsletter and magazine subscriptions are print products — typically special reports. They can be mailed through the U.S. Postal Service as hard copies or made available for download online as PDF files. Here are some of the more popular premiums for newsletter and info product marketing: The super-premium. A super-premium is a special report that delivers all or most of the information, secrets, or strategies promised in the mailing piece. Example: A magalog for Weiss’s Safe Money Report offers a super-premium, “Grow Up to 1,000% Richer in the Great Stock Market Panic of 2002,” that delivers on the big promise of the mailing. The offer of the super-premium is made on just about every other page of the 24-page magalog. The owner’s manual. An owner’s manual advises the subscriber how to use the service for maximum results and benefits. An options trading program, for instance, will typically have a premium explaining terms (e.g., “puts” vs. “calls”) and the types of trades the service makes (e.g., “straddles”). The vertical premium. A vertical premium is a report covering, in depth, one specific area the newsletter deals with rather than the bigger picture. A newsletter on Information Technology, for instance, might have a special report on supply chain management (SCM) or enterprise resource planning (ERP). The resource guide. A resource guide is a mini-directory of vendors, suppliers, associations, websites, and other resources of interest to the newsletter’s target audience. Be sure to include addresses, phone numbers, e-mail addresses, and Web URLs for listed resources. Surveys. The results of subscriber surveys are of great interest to potential subscribers. When Hospital Admitting Monthly added the offer of a salary survey premium, response to its control mailing jumped 50%. “Best of’s.” If you have a regular column that is highly popular with subscribers, collect a dozen or so of them in a “best of” premium. Newsletters covering regulatory or legal issues have done this with monthly columns on court cases and their outcomes (e.g., “The Best of ‘You Be the Judge’”). The editor’s magnum opus. Be careful of offering a book by the editor as a premium, especially if the book is a bestseller or the newsletter is expensive. If the book is a bestseller, many potential subscribers will already own it. If the newsletter is expensive, you’re better off offering a premium with a higher perceived value than a book. E-zines. If you send weekly e-mail updates between monthly print issues, talk about the “free e-zine” they get as a bonus for subscribing. E-alerts. Some newsletters offer periodic, unscheduled e-mails when there is important news or instructions that cannot wait for the next print issue or ezine. If you do this, position it as a value-added premium service. Online archives. Access to your password-protected subscribers-only website is a bonus for subscribers to your print or online newsletter. One feature that subscribers look for is an online archive of back issues. If it is searchable by keyword, even better. Forums and chat groups. Hosting a forum, chat group, or other online community where subscribers can network and share best practices is another nice little online extra. The postings are also very helpful for your marketing and editorial people. Telephone hotlines. Many monthly newsletters offer subscribers a telephone hotline they can call to hear current news and advice. Such hotlines are typically updated weekly. Conference invitations. You can offer potential subscribers invitations to exclusive conferences, workshops, and seminars. They should get these invitations early, before the general public — and a subscriber’s discount on the registration fee wouldn’t hurt. Transcripts. Transcripts of conferences, seminars, teleseminars, webinars, speeches, lectures, even TV or radio appearances by the editor can make attractive premiums. Audio CDs and DVDs. You can tape your editorial staff when they give presentations and offer audios or videos as premiums. Videos have a higher perceived value. I prefer audiotapes because busy people can listen to them in the car. CD-ROMs. A CD-ROM can present multimedia material that’s difficult to reprint in a printed report. The CD-ROM that comes with my book Public Relations Kit for Dummies, for example, includes samples of video news conferences. Software. At least one financial newsletter I’ve seen recently includes trading software as a premium for new subscribers. Software has a high perceived value. Is there a simple spreadsheet, such as a cost calculator, that you can put on a disk or CD-ROM and offer as a premium? Three-ring binders. For a newsletter that has lasting shelf value as a reference, you can offer a free three-ring binder that the subscriber can use to store all his issues in one convenient location. Merchandise. Merchandise, a common premium for magazine subscriptions, is seldom used in newsletter promotions. There are rare exceptions. Release 1.0, a technology newsletter aimed at high-level decision-making executives, offers a Release 1.0 baseball cap as a “payment with order” premium. Consumer magazines are more likely than newsletters to offer merchandise premiums. For many years, Business Week gave away a free solar calculator with a subscription to the magazine. Sports Illustrated offered a free video of the photo shoot for its annual swimsuit issue. 6 Steps to Irresistible Offers The more of the following characteristics your offer incorporates, the more irresistible it will be, and the higher your response rates: 1. Different or unique. The best offers are fresh and new. When copywriter Bill Jayme wrote the direct-mail package that launched New York magazine, he proposed a sweepstakes. Sweepstakes had long been used to sell magazine subscriptions, but none had ever offered the prize Jayme dreamed up: dinner at Gracie Mansion with New York City’s mayor. Most investment newsletters offer free special reports as premiums. The Sovereign Society, a newsletter on offshore investing, offered something different: a free Swiss bank account — a gift not given by any other investment newsletter. Most business magazines offer either discounted subscription rates or standard premiums like special reports, tote bags, or calculators. Advertising Age had a successful control where the premium was a ceramic coffee mug. Coffee mugs are nothing special. But this one was imprinted with a mock-up of an Ad Age cover. If the subscriber was Jan Smith, the headline on the mock issue of Ad Age was personalized to read: “Jan Smith Chosen as Marketing Genius of the Year.” 2. Desirable. An unusual offer works only if it’s something people really want. The Sports Illustrated swimsuit video is a great example. Every red-blooded American male who wasn’t dead would have liked to see it. Sex sells! Another example: A publisher was selling a loose-leaf service on how to manage Novell NetWare local area networks. Response rates doubled when a new direct-mail promotion offered a disk with free software — a collection of utilities for Novell networks. The 100 percent increase in orders confirmed that these software programs were tools network administrators obviously wanted to get their hands on. The outer envelope teaser read: “Yours FREE! — 5 Powerful Programs to Help You Manage Your Novell NetWare Network More Efficiently and Easily — See Inside for Details on This Special TimeLimited Offer.” On the other hand, when a financial newsletter mailed a renewal promotion that offered as a premium a pack of playing cards with the editor’s picture on them, it flopped. No surprise. Who would want that? 3. Has a high perceived value, especially in relation to your fulfillment cost. Free software has traditionally worked well as a premium. Software has a high perceived value in relation to the cost of the goods. In a store or online, software packages can easily sell for $49 to $300 or more. Yet a CD with code on it can be duplicated for about a dollar. That’s why the promotion offering a pack of playing cards with the newsletter editor’s picture on them didn’t work. After all, how much do you pay for a deck of playing cards at your local stationery store? About a dollar, right? Therefore, the perceived value of the playing cards was only a dollar — hardly a motivator to renew a newsletter subscription that costs $79 a year. In a promotion tied in with their sponsorship of the Olympics, IBM offered a special IBM Olympic pin as a premium. In reality, the pin probably only cost (and was worth) a buck or so. But the mailer copy hinted that it could become a collectible, creating the impression of potentially high value. 4. Dramatizes the brand or USP. The symbol for offshore investing has long been Swiss bank accounts. Therefore, the offer of a free Swiss bank account with a subscription to The Sovereign Society supported and dramatized the newsletter’s USP: making money and increasing privacy by investing offshore in things like Swiss bank accounts. Even when the offer does not at first glance seem closely related to the product, a clever copywriter can find a connection. Example: Years ago, Newsweek offered a free radio as a premium for new subscribers. It would seem that a radio was a poor choice for a premium: In the news area, radio and magazines compete with one another. But copywriter Milt Pierce used the differences between these media to make a logical connection between the premium and the product: Dear Reader: What’s the fastest way to get the news? It’s on the radio. That’s why Newsweek wants you to have — as an introductory gift for new subscribers — this superb AM/FM radio. But what’s the best way to get the news? You won’t get just headlines and a rough outline of the news, with Newsweek; you’ll get the news in depth … 5. Easy to take advantage of. You should make it as easy and convenient as possible for the prospect to accept your offer.
